acciaio.etymology: Continues Late Latin aciārium ('steely edge, steel'), derived from Latin acĭēs ('sharp edge, keen blade').

accordare.etymology: Continues Vulgar Latin *accordāre (from cor, cordis, 'heart', meaning 'to bring into harmony'), re-associated in music with corda ('instrument string').

accordo.etymology: Deverbal noun from accordare (< Vulgar Latin *accordāre, from cor, cordis, 'heart'), later aligned in musical terminology with corda ('string').

aceto.etymology: Continues Latin acētum ('sour wine, vinegar'), substantivised neuter past participle linked to acēre ('to be sour').

acqua.etymology: Continues Latin aqua ('water'), with regular Tuscan gemination of the labiovelar stop before /w/ (/ˈakkwa/, spelled cq).

alba.etymology: Continues Vulgar Latin *(lūx) alba ('white morning light'), feminine of Classical Latin albus ('matt white').

albero.etymology: Continues Latin arbŏr, arbŏrem ('tree'), with regular dissimilation of the first r to l (*albor).

alone.etymology: Continues Late Latin halō, halōnis ('luminous ring around sun or moon'), from Greek ἅλως (hálōs, 'threshing floor; circular disc, halo').

amico.etymology: Continues Latin amīcus ('friend'), built on the root of amāre ('to love').

andare.etymology: Suppletive verb combining two roots: forms in and- (probably from Vulgar Latin *ambitāre, frequentative of ambīre, 'to go around') and singular/3rd-plural present vad-/va- from Latin vādere.

aprire.etymology: Continues syncopated Latin aperīre ('to open, uncover'), with past participle aperto continuing apertus.

arrivederci.etymology: Compound of a ('until, to') + rivedere ('to see again', re- + vedere from Latin vidēre) + reciprocal pronoun ci ('each other'): literally 'until seeing each other again'.

aspettare.etymology: Continues Latin exspectāre ('to look out for, await'), crossed in spoken Latin with aspectāre ('to watch attentively').

autunno.etymology: Learned and semi-popular continuation of Latin autumnus ('autumn, harvest season'), with assimilation of -mn- > -nn-.

avere.etymology: Continues Latin habēre ('to hold, possess, have'), developing both possession/idiomatic senses and auxiliary duty in compound past tenses.

azzurro.etymology: Entered Medieval Italian via Arabic lāzaward and Persian lāžward ('lapis lazuli'), with loss of initial l- reinterpreted as the romance definite article.

baule.etymology: Early modern Romance word (parallel to French bahut and Spanish baúl) for a domed wooden travel chest or storage trunk.

bere.etymology: Contracted from older Tuscan bevere (< Latin bibere, 'to drink'), whose stem bev- survives throughout the inflected forms (bevo, bevi, bevuto).

binario.etymology: From Late Latin bīnārius ('consisting of two, paired', from bīnī, 'two by two'), naming the pair of parallel iron rails—and hence a station platform.

biscotto.etymology: Continues Medieval Latin panis biscŏctus ('bread baked twice', bis + cŏctus from cŏquĕre), originally dry ship's rusk baked for long keeping.

bordo.etymology: Entered Italian via Old French bord from Frankish *bord ('ship's side, plank, rim'), cognate with English board.

bosco.etymology: Continues Medieval Latin bŭscus / *bŏscus ('woodland, copse'), of West Germanic origin (*busk, cognate with English bush and German Busch).

braccio.etymology: Continues Latin brāchĭum ('forearm, arm'), borrowed from Greek βραχίων (brakhíōn); plural le braccia continues the Latin neuter plural brāchĭa.

buccia.etymology: Probably from Late Latin *bŭllĕa or pre-Latin Mediterranean stock crossed with lobia ('pod, husk'), attested in Tuscan since the 14th century for fruit rind and tree bark.

buonasera.etymology: Compound of buona ('good', f.) + sera ('evening', from Latin sēra [diēs], 'late part of the day').

buongiorno.etymology: Univerbation of buon ('good', from Latin bonus) + giorno ('day', from Late Latin diurnum), literally wishing someone a good day.

burro.etymology: Via Old French burre from Latin būtyrum and Ancient Greek boútyron ('cow-cheese'); replaced older Tuscan butirro in everyday Italian.

caffè.etymology: Entered Italian (first through Venice in the late sixteenth century) from Ottoman Turkish kahve and Arabic qahwa, naming both the roasted bean drink and the coffeehouse.

caldo.etymology: Continues syncopated Latin caldus for classical calidus ('warm, hot', related to calēre), already noted by Roman grammarians as everyday spoken Latin.

camera.etymology: From Latin camera (borrowed from Ancient Greek kamára, 'vaulted chamber, arched roof'), shifting to mean a private room or hotel bedroom.

camminare.etymology: From Late Latin cammināre ('to travel along a road, walk'), a denominal verb derived from Vulgar Latin cammīnus ('way, path'), borrowed from Gaulish *camminos ('step, way').
camminare.notes: Cognate with French cheminer and Spanish caminar; replaced Classical Latin ambulāre as the everyday Italian verb for walking.

cammino.etymology: From Vulgar Latin cammīnus ('way, road, path'), borrowed from Gaulish *camminos ('step, journey'), from Proto-Celtic *kanxsman ('step').
cammino.notes: Masculine noun (il cammino, 'path, journey'); the 1st-person present form of camminare ('io cammino') shares its spelling.

camomilla.etymology: Continues Late Latin chamomĭlla (alteration of chamaemēlon), from Greek χαμαίμηλον (khamaímēlon, 'earth-apple', named for the apple-like scent of its blossoms).

cantina.etymology: Derived within Italian (probably from canto, 'corner, secluded nook', with suffix -ina) to name a cool underground storage cellar or wine cellar.

cardine.etymology: Continues Latin cardō, cardĭnis ('door pivot, hinge, pole of the sky'), from the accusative cardĭnem.

carota.etymology: Continues Latin carōta ('carrot'), borrowed from Greek καρωτόν (karōtón).

cartella.etymology: Diminutive formation in -ella on Italian carta ('paper, document', < Latin charta < Greek χάρτης, khártēs, 'papyrus sheet').

casa.etymology: Continues Latin casa (originally a modest 'cottage, hut'), which supplanted classical domus across Romance languages as the general word for house and home.

caviglia.etymology: Through Old Provençal cavilha from Vulgar Latin *clavĭcŭla (for Classical clavīcŭla, 'small peg or bolt', diminutive of clāvis), applied anatomically to the anklebone.

centimetro.etymology: Learned metric compound borrowed via French centimètre (1795), from Latin centum ('hundred') + Greek μέτρον (métron, 'measure').

ceramica.etymology: Borrowed via French céramique from Greek κεραμική (τέχνη) (keramikḗ, 'potter's art'), from κέραμος (kéramos, 'potter's clay, earthenware').

cerniera.etymology: Borrowed from Old French charniere ('hinge, pivot'), continuing Late Latin *cardĭnāria from Latin cardō, cardĭnis ('door pivot, hinge').

cesto.etymology: Continues Latin cĭsta ('woven basket, chest'), borrowed from Greek κίστη (kístē, 'wicker basket').

chiave.etymology: Continues Latin clāvem (accusative of clāvis, 'key', related to claudere, 'to close'), with regular Italian palatalization of initial cl- > chi- (/kj/).

chiavistello.etymology: Tuscan alteration (crossed with chiave, 'key') of Vulgar Latin *clāvicĕllus, diminutive of Latin clāvis ('key, locking bar').

chilo.etymology: Shortening of chilogrammo, borrowed from French kilogramme (1795), coined from Greek χίλιοι (khílioi, 'thousand') + γράμμα (grámma, 'gram, small weight').

chiudere.etymology: Continues Vulgar Latin *clūdere (modelled on compounds like inclūdere, exclūdere from classical claudere, 'to close'), with regular cl- > chi-.

ciao.etymology: Borrowed from Venetian s-ciao / s-ciavo ('[your] servant'), from Medieval Latin sclavus; generalized across Italy as an informal greeting for both hello and goodbye.

colazione.etymology: From Latin collātiōnem ('bringing together, monastic light meal read aloud together'), shifting in modern standard Italian to mean breakfast (prima colazione).

colla.etymology: Continues Late Latin cŏlla ('glue, paste'), borrowed from Greek κόλλα (kólla, 'hide or fish glue').

collina.etymology: Continues Latin collīna ('hilly ground, small hill'), feminine substantivisation of collīnus from cŏllis ('hill').

colore.etymology: Continues Latin colōr, colōrem ('hue, complexion, colour').

comporre.etymology: Continues Latin compōnĕre ('to put together, arrange, write music or verse'), syncopated in Tuscan to comporre like porre < pōnĕre.

corda.etymology: Continues Latin chŏrda ('gut string of a lyre; cord'), from Greek χορδή (khordḗ, 'gut, musical string').

corridoio.etymology: Derived from correre ('to run', from Latin currere) with the place suffix -toio/-doio: originally a long passage along which one could run between rooms or fortifications.

cortile.etymology: Derived from corte ('court, enclosed yard', from Latin cohortem / cōrtem) with the suffix -ile, naming the open inner courtyard of an Italian palazzo or inn.

crema.etymology: Entered Italian via Old French cresme, blending Late Latin chrisma ('anointing salve', < Greek χρῖσμα) with Gaulish *crama ('milk skimmings').

crescere.etymology: Continues Latin crēscĕre ('to come into being, grow, increase'), an inchoative verb in -sc-.

cucchiaio.etymology: Continues Latin cochlĕārium ('spoon originally used for eating snails and eggs'), derived from cochlĕa ('snail shell').

cuocere.etymology: Continues Vulgar Latin *cŏcĕre (for Classical Latin cŏquĕre, 'to cook, bake, ripen'), with regular Tuscan diphthongisation of stressed open ŏ.

dire.etymology: Continues shortened Late Latin dīre for classical dīcere ('to say, tell'), keeping the dic- stem in dico, dici, dice, diciamo.

dito.etymology: Continues Latin dĭgĭtum ('finger, pointer'); the collective feminine plural le dita reflects the Late Latin neuter plural dĭgĭta for the fingers as a set.

domani.etymology: Continues Late Latin dē māne ('in the early morning'), shifting from 'early next morning' to 'tomorrow'.

donna.etymology: Continues Latin dŏmĭna ('mistress of the household, lady'), syncopated in Vulgar Latin to *domna with assimilation -mn- > -nn-.

dormire.etymology: Continues Latin dormīre ('to sleep') directly in both spelling and conjugation.

dovere.etymology: Continues Latin dēbēre ('to owe; to be bound to'), with labialization of unstressed pretonic e to o before v.

dozzina.etymology: Derived from dodici ('twelve', < Latin duŏdĕcim) via Old Italian dozzina / Provençal dotzena ('group of twelve').

e.etymology: Continues Latin et ('and'), losing final -t before consonants while preserving optional ed before vowels.

edera.etymology: Continues Latin hĕdĕra ('ivy'), with regular loss of initial h- and preservation of open tonic /ɛ/.

essere.etymology: Continues Latin esse ('to be') via Vulgar Latin *essere, blending forms from Latin esse and sedēre/stāre (such as past participle stato from status).

etichetta.etymology: Borrowed from French étiquette ('small paper ticket or label attached to a dossier; court protocol'), from Middle Dutch stikken ('to stick, pin').

faggio.etymology: Continues Vulgar Latin *fāgĕus, adjective from Classical Latin fāgus ('beech tree'), cognate with English beech and German Buche.

famiglia.etymology: Continues Latin familia ('household', from famulus), shifting from an entire household estate to close kin.

fare.etymology: Continues shortened Late Latin fare for classical facere ('to make, do'), retaining the fac- stem in forms such as faccio, facciamo, facevo, and fatto (< factum).

feltro.etymology: Early Germanic loanword into Late Latin (*filtrum, cognate with Old High German filz and English felt) denoting matted, unspun wool.

fermo.etymology: Continues Latin firmus ('steady, solid, resolute'), keeping both physical ('still, motionless') and figurative ('firm') meanings.

fessura.etymology: Continues Latin fissūra ('cleft, narrow chink, crack'), from fissus, past participle of findĕre ('to split, cleave').

fianco.etymology: Entered Romance via Frankish *hlanka ('hip, flank, bend of the body'), via Old French flanc with regular Italian outcomes fl- > fi-.

fiero.etymology: Continues Latin fĕrus ('untamed, spirited, bold'), whose chivalric sense shifted via Old French fier toward 'noble, proud'.

finestra.etymology: Continues Latin fenestra ('window, opening for light'), with raising of unstressed e to i in the initial syllable.

fornello.etymology: Diminutive in -ello of forno ('oven, furnace', < Latin fŭrnus), designating a small brazier or kitchen stove burner.

fradicio.etymology: Metathesised Tuscan outcome (via *fracĭdus) of Latin fracĭdus ('overripe, sodden, softened by moisture'), from fracēre.

fratello.etymology: Continues Latin frātellum, originally an affectionate diminutive of frāter ('brother') that replaced bare frate in everyday kinship.

freddo.etymology: Continues syncopated Vulgar Latin *frigdu(m) for classical frīgidus ('cold'), with assimilation of -gd- > -dd-.

furbo.etymology: Originally Renaissance jargon furbo ('pickpocket, streetwise rogue', via French fourbe linked to fourbir, 'to polish/clean out'), later softened to 'clever, smart'.

gesso.etymology: Continues Latin gy̆psum ('gypsum, plaster, chalk'), borrowed from Greek γύψος (gýpsos), with regular assimilation of -ps- > -ss-.

ghiaccio.etymology: Continues Vulgar Latin *glăcĭum (masculine reshaping of Classical feminine glăcĭēs, 'ice'), with regular outcome gl- > ghi- and -cj- > -cci-.

giardino.etymology: Borrowed from Old French jardin ('garden'), itself from Frankish *gardo ('enclosure, yard').

giornale.etymology: Substantivised use of the adjective giornale (< Latin diurnālis, 'daily', from diēs, 'day'), originally foglio giornale ('daily sheet').

giovedì.etymology: Continues Latin Iŏvis diēs ('Jove's day, day of Jupiter'), fused into a single oxytone compound like lunedì through venerdì.

grazie.etymology: Plural of grazia, from Latin grātia ('favour, goodwill, thanks'), shortened from phrases like tante grazie / rendo grazie ('I render thanks').

guscio.etymology: Probably continues Vulgar Latin *cŭscĭum / Greek κυστίον (kystíon, 'little bladder, pod, husk'), with sonorisation of initial k- > g-.

ieri.etymology: Continues Latin herī ('yesterday'), with regular diphthongization of stressed open e to ie (/ˈjɛri/).

imparare.etymology: Continues Vulgar Latin *imparāre (in- + parāre, 'to acquire, prepare for oneself, store in the mind').

impastare.etymology: Prefixed verb formed in Late/Medieval Latin (impastāre) from in- + pasta ('dough, paste', < Greek πάστη).

in.etymology: Continues Latin in ('in, into, on'), expressing spatial enclosure, country/region location, transport (in treno), and states.

lampo.etymology: Deverbal noun from Old Italian lampare ('to flash, gleam'), continuing Late Latin lampāre from Greek λάμπειν (lámpein, 'to shine').

latte.etymology: Continues Vulgar Latin *lactem (for classical neuter lac, stem lact-, 'milk'), with assimilation of -ct- > -tt- and masculine gender in Italian.

lavagna.etymology: Named after Lavagna on the Ligurian coast near Genoa, historic quarry center for the dark splitting slate used in school boards and roofs.

leggio.etymology: Derived from leggere ('to read', < Latin lĕgĕre) with the instrument/place suffix -ìo, denoting a slanted stand for holding books or sheet music.

lente.etymology: Continues Latin lēns, lĕntem ('lentil'), transferred in 13th-century Italian optics to convex glass discs shaped like a lentil seed.

lenticchia.etymology: Continues Latin lentĭcŭla ('little lentil'), diminutive of lēns, lĕntis ('lentil', source also of lente, 'glass lens').

lettera.etymology: Continues Latin littera ('alphabetic character'; plural litterae, 'written epistle, letter'), uniting both meanings in singular Italian lettera.

limone.etymology: Entered medieval Italian through Mediterranean trade from Arabic laymūn and Persian līmūn.

lo.etymology: Develops from Latin illum, accusative masculine singular of the demonstrative ille ('that'), losing its initial syllable in unstressed proclitic position.

locanda.etymology: From the Latin gerundive phrase (domus) locanda, '(a house) to be let/rented out', from locāre ('to place, rent out')—originally written on signs outside inns.

lunedì.etymology: Continues Latin lūnae diēs ('day of the Moon'), fusing the genitive lūnae with dì (< diēs).

mandorla.etymology: Continues Late Latin amandŭla (alteration of Classical amygdăla, from Greek ἀμυγδάλη, amygdálē, 'almond'), with apheresis of initial a-.

mangiare.etymology: Borrowed via Old French mangier from Spoken Latin mandūcāre ('to chew, eat heartily'), which replaced classical edere.

manica.etymology: Continues Latin manĭca ('long tunic sleeve covering the hand'), derived from mănus ('hand').

manico.etymology: Continues Late Latin *manĭcus ('handle, grip'), built on Latin mănus ('hand'), literally 'the part held in the hand'.

mansarda.etymology: Borrowed from French mansarde, named after the seventeenth-century French architect François Mansart, who popularized habitable rooms beneath pitched roofs.

mattina.etymology: Substantivized feminine of Latin mātūtīna (hōra), '(hour) of Matuta', the Roman goddess of the dawn.

melodia.etymology: Continues Late Latin melōdĭa, from Greek μελῳδία (melōidía, 'singing, choral song'), compound of μέλος (mélos, 'musical phrase') + ᾠδή (ōidḗ, 'song').

mescolare.etymology: Continues Vulgar Latin *misculāre, frequentative/diminutive derivative of Classical Latin miscēre ('to mix, mingle').

messaggio.etymology: Borrowed via Old Provençal messatge / Old French message from Vulgar Latin *missātĭcum ('that which is sent'), from Latin mĭttĕre ('to send').

mezzanotte.etymology: Univerbation of mezza notte, continuing Latin mĕdĭa nŏx / mĕdĭam nŏctem ('middle of the night').

mezzogiorno.etymology: Transparent compound of mezzo ('half, middle', from Latin medius) + giorno ('day'), naming twelve noon (and, by extension, southern Italy where the midday sun stands).

miele.etymology: Continues Latin mel, stem mell- ('honey'), diphthongizing stressed open e to ie in open syllable.

moneta.etymology: Continues Latin monēta ('mint; coin'), from the temple of Iūnō Monēta on Rome's Capitoline Hill where silver coins were struck.

montagna.etymology: Continues Vulgar Latin *montānĕa (neuter plural of montānĕus, 'of mountains', treated as a feminine singular collective), derived from Latin mōns, mŏntis.

muscolo.etymology: Learned/semi-learned continuation of Latin mūscŭlus ('little mouse; muscle', comparing the rippling of a flexed biceps under the skin to a mouse).

neve.etymology: Continues Latin nĭx, nĭvem ('snow'), from the accusative nĭvem with regular Romance development ĭ > closed /e/.

niente.etymology: Exact Latin source debated; Treccani notes several proposals—most prominently Vulgar Latin *nec gentem ('not a soul/person') or *ne inde—with medieval Tuscan variants neente and neiente.

no.etymology: Continues Latin nōn in stressed standalone position, whereas unstressed proclitic position before a verb preserved the final nasal as non.

non.etymology: Continues Latin nōn (itself from Old Latin noenum, 'not one'). In Italian it stands directly before the verb phrase to negate a clause.

nonna.etymology: Continues Late Latin nŏnna ('revered elder woman, nun, grandmother'), an affectionate nursery reduplication.

nonno.etymology: Continues Late Latin nonnus (originally a respectful address to an elder or monk), which replaced classical avus as the everyday word for grandfather.

occhiale.etymology: Derived from occhio ('eye', < Latin oculus); plural gli occhiali ('eyeglasses') was coined in late-thirteenth-century Italy where wearable spectacles were first crafted.

odore.etymology: Continues Latin odōr, odōrem ('smell, scent, fragrance'), cognate with Greek ὄζω (ózō, 'to smell').

ok.etymology: Twentieth-century international borrowing from American English O.K. / okay, used in spoken Italian as an informal check or agreement.

olio.etymology: Continues Latin ŏlĕum ('olive oil'), an ancient Mediterranean word borrowed alongside Greek ἔλαιον (élaion).

oliva.etymology: Continues Latin ŏlīva ('olive fruit; olive tree'), early borrowing from archaic Greek *ἐλαίϝα (*elaíwa).

ombra.etymology: Continues Latin ŭmbra ('shadow, shade'), with regular Tuscan opening of tonic short ŭ to closed /o/.

ordinare.etymology: Continues Latin ōrdĭnāre ('to set in rows, arrange, command'), built on ōrdō, ōrdĭnis ('row, order').

ordine.etymology: Continues Latin ōrdinem (accusative of ōrdō, 'row, arrangement, command'), originally a weaving term for threads in a loom.

orecchio.etymology: Continues Latin aurĭcŭla (diminutive of auris, 'ear') via masculine reshaping *aurĭcŭlum, with au- > o- and -cl- > -cchi-.

orologiaio.etymology: Derived with agent suffix -aio (< Latin -ārius) from orologio ('clock, watch', < Latin hōrolŏgĭum < Greek ὡρολόγιον, 'hour-teller').

orologio.etymology: Continues Latin hōrologium (from Ancient Greek hōrológion, 'hour-teller', from hṓra 'hour' + légein 'to tell').

ospite.etymology: Continues Latin hospitem (accusative of hospes), which already denoted both partners of hospitality—the host who welcomes and the guest who is welcomed.

ottava.etymology: Feminine substantivisation of ottavo (< Latin octāvus, 'eighth', from ŏctō, 'eight'), short for ottava corda or ottava nota.

pagnotta.etymology: Formed on pane ('bread', < Latin pānis) with diminutive/round-shape suffix -otta (*paniotta), denoting a single round loaf.

palazzo.etymology: From Latin Palātium (the Palatine Hill in Rome, site of the imperial residences), broadening in Italian cities to mean any multi-storey masonry town building.

pane.etymology: Continues Latin pānem (accusative of pānis, 'bread'), shared with compagno ('companion', literally one who shares bread).

parlare.etymology: Continues Christian Late Latin parabolāre ('to speak in parables, converse', from Greek parabolḗ), which became the everyday word for speaking in Italian and French.

pasta.etymology: Continues Late Latin pasta ('kneaded dough, paste'), from Greek πάστη (pástē, 'barley porridge, salted meal').

pennello.etymology: Continues Latin pēnicĭllus ('small tail; painter's tuft brush'), double diminutive of pēnis ('tail').

perno.etymology: Continues Latin pĕrna ('ham, leg, wooden tenon or pivot shaped like a haunch') via Vulgar Latin *pĕrnum.

pianoforte.etymology: Shortened from gravicembalo col piano e col forte ('harpsichord with soft and loud'), coined in Florence by Bartolomeo Cristofori around 1700 for his hammer-action keyboard instrument.

piazza.etymology: Continues Latin platĕa ('broad street, open courtyard'), borrowed from Greek πλατεῖα (plateîa, 'wide way'), with regular Italian development of -tj- > -zz- and pl- > pi-.

piede.etymology: Continues Latin pēs, pĕdem ('foot'), with regular Tuscan diphthongisation of stressed open ĕ in an open syllable (pĕde > piede).

pioggia.etymology: Continues Vulgar Latin *ploia for classical pluvia ('rain', from pluere, 'to rain'), with pl- > pi- and -vj- > -ddʒ-.

piolo.etymology: Tuscan derivative (via *pediŏlum) of Latin pĕdĭcŭlus / pēs ('little foot, support peg, rung').

pomodoro.etymology: 16th-century compound of pomo d'oro ('golden apple'), naming the first yellow-fruited varieties brought from the Americas to Renaissance Italy.

ponte.etymology: Continues Latin pontem (accusative of pōns, 'bridge'), keeping masculine gender in Italian (il ponte).

porcellana.etymology: Originally the Old Italian name of the glossy cowrie shell (porcellana, from porcella, 'little sow'), extended by Marco Polo to translucent Chinese ceramic whose glaze resembled the shell.

porta.etymology: Continues Latin porta ('city gate, doorway'), from the Indo-European root *per- ('to pass through'), cognate with porto ('harbour') and English port.

potere.etymology: Continues Vulgar Latin *potēre, regularized from classical posse ('to be able', contraction of potis esse).

prego.etymology: First-person singular of pregare ('to pray, ask earnestly'), from Latin precārī; shortened from vi/La prego ('I beg you / please do') into Italian's all-purpose courteous reply.

primavera.etymology: Continues Vulgar Latin *prīma vēra, from Classical Latin prīmō vēre ('at the start of spring', from prīmus 'first' and vēr 'spring').

qui.etymology: Continues Vulgar Latin *(ec)cu(m) hīc ('behold here'), parallel to qua from *(ec)cu(m) hāc.

ramo.etymology: Continues Latin rāmus ('tree branch, bough'), from the accusative rāmum.

ritmo.etymology: Continues Latin rhythmus, from Greek ῥυθμός (rhythmós, 'measured flow, cadence, proportion'), related to ῥέω ('to flow').

rotolo.etymology: Continues Late Latin rŏtŭlus ('little wheel, scroll, roll'), diminutive of Latin rŏta ('wheel').

sabato.etymology: Continues Christian Latin sabbătum, borrowed via Greek σάββατον (sábbaton) from Hebrew šabbāth ('day of rest', from šābath, 'to cease from work').

sale.etymology: Continues Latin sāl, sălem ('salt'), pan-Indo-European root *séh₂ls shared with English salt and German Salz.

scaffale.etymology: Probably derived from Medieval Latin *scapha / Lombardic *skafa ('wooden tub, shelf, board'), originally designating an open set of wooden shelves for books or wares.

scala.etymology: Continues Latin scāla ('ladder, flight of steps'), related to scandere ('to climb'); used in Italian for stairs, ladders, and musical scales.

scusare.etymology: Continues Latin excūsāre ('to release from a charge, excuse', from ex- + causa), losing unstressed initial ex- > s-.

secchio.etymology: Masculine back-formation beside secchia, continuing Late Latin sĭtŭla ('water bucket, well pail') via syncopated Vulgar Latin *sĭcla.

sedia.etymology: Derived within Italian from sedere ('to sit', < Latin sedēre), naming a backed chair.

sera.etymology: From Latin sēra (diēs), feminine of sērus ('late'), naming the late hours of the day as daylight fades.

settimana.etymology: Continues Late Latin septimāna ('period of seven days'), derived from septem ('seven').

sgabello.etymology: Continues Latin scabĕllum / scamĭllum ('low footstool, step bench'), diminutive related to scamnum ('bench'), with voicing of sc- > sg-.

silenzio.etymology: Learned and popular continuation of Latin silentium ('silence, stillness'), from silēre ('to be silent').

solo.etymology: The adjective continues Latin sōlus ('alone, single'), while the adverbial sense 'only, just' continues Latin sōlum.

specchio.etymology: Continues Latin speculum ('mirror', from specere, 'to look at'), with syncope of unstressed u (speclu) and regular -cl- > -kkj-.

spendere.etymology: Continues Latin expendĕre ('to weigh out money, pay out'), with apheresis of initial ex-, from pendĕre ('to weigh').

spugna.etymology: Continues Latin spŏngĭa ('sea sponge'), borrowed from Greek σπογγιά (spongiá), with regular Tuscan palatalisation of -ngj- to /ɲɲ/.

stagista.etymology: Formed in modern Italian from French stage ('training placement', ultimately related to Old French estage, 'dwelling, period of residence') plus the agentive suffix -ista.

stare.etymology: Continues Latin stāre ('to stand, remain firm'), expanding in Italian to cover staying in a place, health/well-being (come stai?), and progressive constructions with the gerund.

stazione.etymology: From Latin statiōnem ('standing place, post, stopping point', from stāre), extended in the railway age to train and bus stations.

stoffa.etymology: Early Romance noun linked to Old French estoffe and Middle High German stouf / Old High German stopfōn ('to stuff, pad, equip with cloth').

tallone.etymology: Continues Vulgar Latin *tālō, *tālōnem, augmentative of Classical Latin tālus ('anklebone, heel').

tavolo.etymology: Masculine back-formation from feminine tavola (< Latin tabula, 'plank, board, table'), distinguishing a piece of furniture (il tavolo) from the laid dining table (a tavola).

tempesta.etymology: Continues Vulgar Latin *tempĕsta (for Classical tempĕstās, tempestātis, 'season, weather, storm'), derived from tĕmpus ('time, weather').

tempo.etymology: Continues Latin tempus ('time, season, weather condition'), which is why one Italian word naturally covers both clock time and the weather.

terracotta.etymology: Compound of terra ('earth, clay', Latin tĕrra) + cotta ('baked, fired', feminine past participle of cuocere < Latin cŏquĕre).

tiglio.etymology: Continues Vulgar Latin *tilius for classical feminine tilia ('linden or lime tree'), prized across Italian courtyards and avenues (viali dei tigli) for its honey-scented June blossoms.

titolo.etymology: Continues Latin tĭtŭlus ('inscription, label, heading of a scroll or book').

torta.etymology: From Late Latin tōrta (panis), originally a round 'twisted' or rolled loaf/pastry (related to torquēre, 'to twist').

treno.etymology: In its railway sense, adapted in the nineteenth century from French train and English train (ultimately from Old French traïner, 'to draw, pull along').

tu.etymology: Continues Latin tū, the inherited Indo-European singular second-person subject pronoun.

tè.etymology: Borrowed via Dutch/French thé from Hokkien (Min Nan) Chinese tê, reflecting maritime trade from Xiamen/Fujian.

uovo.etymology: Continues Latin ovum ('egg'), preserving the Latin neuter plural ending -a in its feminine Italian plural le uova.

valigia.etymology: Attested in medieval Italian (valigia) and borrowed into French as valise; of debated Late Latin or Arabic origin, naming a rider's or traveller's bag.

valzer.etymology: 19th-century loanword from German Walzer ('waltz'), agent noun from walzen ('to revolve, glide in circles').

vaso.etymology: Continues Latin vāsum (collateral masculine form of neuter vās, 'vessel, container, pot').

vassoio.etymology: Continues Late Latin missōrĭum / *vassōrĭum (crossed with vas, 'vessel, dish'), originally a flat wooden winnowing or serving tray.

vedere.etymology: Continues Latin vidēre ('to see'), with regular lowering of short Latin i to closed e in vedere.

venerdì.etymology: Continues Latin Veneris diēs ('day of Venus'), preserving the ancient planetary week in everyday speech.

venire.etymology: Continues Latin venīre ('to come'), preserving palatalized velar forms like vengo (< veniō) alongside diphthongized viene (< venit).

veramente.etymology: Formed within Italian from the feminine adjective vera ('true', from Latin vēra) plus the adverbial suffix -mente (originally Latin ablative mente, 'with a ... mind').

via.etymology: Continues Latin via ('road, way, street') unchanged in spelling; also used adverbially ('away, off') from phrases like andare per via.

volere.etymology: Continues reconstructed Vulgar Latin *volēre, regularized from classical Latin velle ('to wish, want') on analogy with present forms like volō.

zia.etymology: Continues Late Latin thĭa ('aunt'), borrowed from Byzantine Greek θεία (theía, feminine of θεῖος, 'uncle').

zucchero.etymology: Borrowed in medieval maritime Italy from Arabic sukkar ('sugar'), ultimately from Sanskrit śarkarā ('gravel, grit, crystal sugar').
